title: GOD COMMANDED ISRAEL TO BURY THEIR HUMAN WASTE—BUT THE REASON GOES FAR DEEPER THAN CLEANLINESS
paragraphs: GOD COMMANDED ISRAEL TO BURY THEIR HUMAN WASTE—BUT THE REASON GOES FAR DEEPER THAN CLEANLINESS
Deuteronomy 23:12–14 reveals a startling truth about God's holiness, the things we leave exposed, and the Savior who went outside the camp to bring sinners back into the presence of God.
There is a command in the Bible so uncomfortable that most preachers will probably never build a sermon around it.
It involves human waste.
A shovel.
A place outside the camp.
And a warning from God that should make every believer stop and think.
Because buried inside this seemingly embarrassing instruction is something profoundly beautiful about the holiness of God, the dignity of human life, and the astonishing grace of Jesus Christ.
But there is also something deeply unsettling.
God told Israel that even their most private bodily functions mattered in the place where He had chosen to dwell among them.
Not because the human body was disgusting.
Not because God was embarrassed by the people He created.
And certainly not because using the bathroom was a sin.
The reason was far more significant.
And once you understand what was happening in that wilderness camp, you may never read the words “God is with you” quite the same way again.
Listen carefully to what Scripture actually says.

“You shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out to it. And you shall have a trowel with your tools, and when you sit down outside, you shall dig a hole with it and turn back and cover up your excrement.”
That is Deuteronomy 23:12–13, translated from the Hebrew.
Then comes the explanation.

“Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you, therefore your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.”
Deuteronomy 23:14, ESV.
Read that last sentence again.
“Your camp must be holy.”
God was talking about human waste.
Yet He connected that ordinary, unavoidable reality of human existence to the holiness of the place where His people lived.
Why?
Imagine yourself standing in the wilderness thousands of years ago.

You are surrounded by tents stretching across the desert. Children are running between families. Mothers are preparing meals. Fathers are gathering supplies. The elderly are resting beneath whatever shade they can find.
There are animals, cooking fires, water containers, and thousands upon thousands of people living in close quarters.
There are no modern toilets.
No underground sewer systems.
No sanitation trucks.
No running water from a kitchen faucet.
And in the middle of this enormous community is something unlike anything the surrounding nations could claim in the same covenantal sense.
The God who delivered Israel from Egypt has chosen to dwell among His people.
The pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire have testified to His guiding presence.
The tabernacle stands as the appointed center of Israel's worship.
The people are not merely surviving in the wilderness.
They are learning how to live as a holy nation before the living God.
And holiness was never intended to remain confined to religious ceremonies.
It reached into their homes.
Their relationships.
Their business dealings.
Their treatment of strangers.
Their sexual conduct.
Their worship.
And yes, even the disposal of their bodily waste.
Because the God of Israel was not interested in being acknowledged only during sacred ceremonies while everyday life remained untouched by His commands.
He was teaching His people that belonging to Him changed how they lived.
Even when nobody was watching.
Even when the matter seemed insignificant.
Even when obedience involved something as ordinary as digging a hole and covering what needed to be covered.
Now look at the Hebrew.
The command in Deuteronomy 23:13 includes the expression:
וְכִסִּיתָ אֶת־צֵאָתֶךָ
Ve-khissita et-tse'atekha.
It means, “And you shall cover your excrement.”
The Hebrew verb comes from כסה (kasah), meaning “to cover.”
The noun צֵאָה (tse'ah) refers to excrement or bodily waste.
There is nothing mysterious about the vocabulary.
God was giving a real instruction about a real physical responsibility.
The waste was to be taken outside the camp, buried, and not left exposed where people lived.

The instruction had obvious practical value. Proper waste disposal helps prevent contamination and the spread of disease, even though the passage does not explain the command using modern germ theory.
But the text itself emphasizes something more than public health.
It gives a theological reason.
כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ מִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּקֶרֶב מַחֲנֶךָ
Ki YHWH Elohekha mithallekh beqerev machanekha.
“Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp.”
The Hebrew expression mithallekh beqerev conveys the LORD's movement or presence among His people.
What a remarkable picture.
The Creator of heaven and earth, the One before whom mountains tremble, the One who divided the sea, is described as walking in the midst of Israel's camp.
And because He is present, the camp must be holy.
Not because human waste has supernatural power to contaminate God's divine nature.
Not because normal bodily functions make a person morally wicked.
But because God was establishing a covenant community in which His holiness shaped even ordinary physical practices.
The passage then uses another striking Hebrew expression:
עֶרְוַת דָּבָר
'Ervat davar.
It can be understood as “an indecent thing” or “something improper or exposed.”
The expression is broader than a simple modern sanitation term. In this context, it concerns something inappropriate being left exposed within a camp that was to be kept holy.
And here is where we must be careful.
It would be easy to turn this passage into a dramatic claim that every hidden sin is represented by human waste.
But that would go beyond what Moses actually said.

Deuteronomy 23:12–14 is first a literal instruction concerning the cleanliness and holiness of Israel's camp, particularly within the wider setting of Deuteronomy 23:9–14 and its regulations for a military encampment.
We must honor that original meaning.
Yet the principle it reveals reaches into a much larger biblical story.
God's presence calls His people to holiness in the ordinary details of life.
And that is where this ancient command begins to confront us.
Because many of us have become skilled at dividing our lives into two worlds.
The part we present to God.
And the part we assume He does not care about.
We pray in public, but speak cruelly in private.
We sing about forgiveness, but quietly nurture bitterness.
We post Scripture, but refuse to apologize to the people we have wounded.
We ask God to bless our families, while withholding love from the very people He has entrusted to us.
We speak about holiness, yet sometimes treat repentance as something we will deal with later.
And somewhere along the way, we begin to believe that if something is hidden from other people, it has somehow become insignificant before God.
But Scripture will not allow us to confuse secrecy with holiness.
Hebrews 4:13 declares:
“Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.” (KJV)
That verse is not about sanitation.
It is about the searching knowledge of God.
And when placed alongside the broader biblical call to holiness, it raises a question that can be painfully personal.
What have you learned to hide from people while refusing to surrender it to Jesus?
Perhaps it is an addiction you keep promising to abandon.
Perhaps it is resentment toward someone who betrayed you.
Perhaps it is a secret habit that leaves you ashamed every time you finish.
Perhaps it is pride disguised as spiritual maturity.
Perhaps you have become so good at looking strong that nobody knows how exhausted your soul has become.
You smile at church.
You answer, “I'm blessed.”
You encourage everybody else.
Then you go home, close the door, and struggle with things you cannot bring yourself to say out loud.
And sometimes the heaviest burden is not simply the struggle itself.
It is the fear that if anyone discovers the truth, they will never look at you the same way again.
But please hear this.
The God who calls you to holiness is also the God who invites you to come into the light.
He is not asking you to pretend you have never fallen.
He is calling you to stop making peace with what is destroying you.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and protecting it.
There is a difference between confessing weakness and celebrating disobedience.
There is a difference between falling and deciding that you no longer need to get up.
First John 1:9 offers a promise to those who confess their sins: God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Notice that word.
Cleanse.
Not merely expose.
Not merely accuse.
Not merely remind you of everything you did wrong.
Cleanse.
And suddenly we begin to see why the larger biblical story matters so much.
Because Deuteronomy's command was not the final word God would speak about holiness, uncleanness, and His dwelling among humanity.
Something greater was coming.
Someone greater was coming.
And His story would take us outside the camp.
But before we get there, consider another Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 23:14.
קָדוֹשׁ
Qadosh.
Holy.
Set apart.
Belonging to God.
The command that the camp must be holy was not an invitation to pretend that Israel had become flawless.
It was a summons to live according to the character and covenant requirements of the God who had redeemed them.
Remember the order of Israel's story.
God did not wait for Israel to become a perfectly organized, morally flawless nation before delivering them from slavery.
He rescued them from Egypt.
Then He taught them how His redeemed people were to live.
Redemption came before their obedience to these wilderness instructions.
That does not make obedience optional.
It makes obedience a response to the God who had already shown them mercy.
And this pattern prepares us to understand the Gospel.
We do not purchase salvation by becoming impressive enough for God.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
But the very next verse says that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave us unchanged.
Grace brings us to the Savior who changes us.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
Because the Bible speaks not only of things being taken outside the camp.
It speaks of people being taken outside the camp.
Under the law of Moses, certain conditions required separation from the camp as part of Israel's ceremonial regulations.
Numbers 5:1–4 addresses the removal of those who were ceremonially unclean under specified circumstances.
Leviticus 13 describes how a person diagnosed with certain serious skin diseases could be required to live outside the camp.
Imagine the loneliness.
Imagine watching people continue their daily lives while you remain separated.
Imagine the ache of wanting to be near your family.
To worship with the community.
To be embraced without fear.
To belong.
Now remember something astonishing about Jesus.
When a man with leprosy approached Him in Mark 1:40–42, the man said:
“If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.”
And Jesus, moved with compassion, stretched out His hand and touched him.
“I will; be thou clean.”
The man was cleansed.
Think about that moment.
Under ordinary human expectations, the man was someone others would avoid.
Yet Jesus reached toward him.
The Holy One was not overwhelmed by the man's condition.
Instead, Christ's healing power restored him.
The man did not cleanse himself first and then earn the right to approach Jesus.
He came to Jesus in his need.
And Jesus had compassion.
That is the Savior we preach.
Not a Savior who celebrates sin.
Not a Savior who denies the reality of holiness.
But a Savior whose mercy is powerful enough to meet the unclean, forgive the guilty, and restore the broken.
And then we reach Hebrews 13.
This is the passage that makes the connection to Deuteronomy's world of camp holiness especially profound.
Hebrews 13:11–12 says:

“For the bodies of those beasts, whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin, are burned without the camp. Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate.” (KJV)
Read those words slowly.
Jesus suffered outside the gate.
The writer of Hebrews is directly drawing on the Old Testament sacrificial system, especially the disposal of certain sin-offering remains outside the camp.
He is not claiming that Jesus fulfilled the command to bury human excrement in some one-to-one symbolic way.
We should never force that interpretation upon Deuteronomy.
But both passages belong to the wider biblical world in which holiness, uncleanness, sacrifice, and the boundary of the camp mattered.
And Hebrews makes a stunning declaration.
Jesus went outside the gate to sanctify His people through His own blood.
The Son of God entered the place of rejection and suffering.
He bore shame.
He endured mockery.
He was wounded.
He was crucified.
Not because He had committed sin.
Scripture says He knew no sin.
But because He came to save sinners.
The One who was perfectly holy willingly suffered the disgrace of the cross so that guilty people could be brought near to God.
Can you see the beauty?
The wilderness camp had to be kept holy because God dwelt among His people.
But humanity's deepest problem could never be solved merely by keeping a campsite clean.
We needed more than a shovel.
More than a regulation.
More than outward order.
We needed a Redeemer.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed hearts made new.
We needed someone who could deal with the guilt and power of sin.
And Jesus Christ came.
He lived the righteous life we failed to live.
He died for our sins.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, those who repent and believe receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
The cross did not make holiness unnecessary.
It revealed both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable cost of our redemption.
God did not simply ignore evil.
Christ gave Himself to rescue us from it.
That is why Hebrews 13:13 continues:
“Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.” (KJV)
There is the invitation.
Go to Him.
Even when following Him costs you the approval of others.
Even when obedience requires you to abandon a cherished sin.
Even when repentance means admitting that the image you have carefully maintained is not the whole truth.
Go to Him.
Not because you can cleanse yourself.
But because He is the Savior who sanctifies His people.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needs to hear tonight.
You do not have to become your own savior before you come to Jesus.
You do have to stop pretending that you do not need one.
There are people reading this who have spent years carrying a private history they cannot undo.
A marriage damaged by betrayal.
A child wounded by words that cannot be taken back.
A season of rebellion.
A habit that slowly became a prison.
A secret failure that still returns in the middle of the night.
And the enemy would love for you to believe that your worst chapter is your permanent identity.
But the Gospel tells another story.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Yet the risen Christ restored him and commissioned him to shepherd His people.
The woman in Luke 7:36–50 approached Jesus with tears and an alabaster jar of ointment, and heard Him speak of forgiveness and faith.
Paul once persecuted the church.
Yet Christ showed him mercy and transformed him into a witness of the Gospel.
Their stories are not permission slips to continue in sin.
They are testimonies that the mercy of Jesus reaches people whose pasts are painfully real.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not that Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not that the consequences of sin always disappear.
Not that every broken relationship is instantly repaired.
But that sin and shame do not have to possess the final word over the person who comes to Christ.
Repentance is real.
Forgiveness is real.
Transformation is real.
And restoration, though it may involve painful honesty, accountability, and a long process of healing, is possible through God's grace.
There is another detail worth noticing.
God commanded Israel to take responsibility for its waste.
The instruction was practical.
Personal.
Unavoidable.
Every individual had a role in preserving the holiness and order of the community.
You could not simply leave your mess for someone else and call that faithfulness.
And although we must not turn a sanitation law into a direct allegory of every spiritual struggle, the broader biblical call to personal responsibility is unmistakable.
Galatians 6:5 says that each person will bear his own load.
James 5:16 speaks of confessing sins and praying for one another.
Ephesians 4 calls believers to put away falsehood, bitterness, and corrupt speech.
Biblical holiness is not just about what we say we believe.
It reaches into what we practice.
How we treat people when we are angry.
Whether we tell the truth when lying would protect our reputation.
Whether we seek forgiveness when our pride tells us to remain silent.
Whether we choose integrity when compromise would be easier.
Whether we love people who cannot repay us.
Whether we honor Christ when nobody is applauding.
And maybe that is why this unusual passage deserves far more attention than it receives.
Because it reminds us that there is no part of ordinary life too small to be lived before God.
Not the workplace.
Not the family dinner table.
Not the phone screen.
Not the private conversation.
Not the decisions made after midnight.
And not even the most basic responsibilities of bodily life.
The Lord of the sanctuary is also Lord of everyday obedience.
But do not misunderstand His holiness as an invitation to live in constant terror that one mistake will make Him abandon you.
For those who belong to Jesus Christ, Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
The God who calls His children to repentance is not asking them to earn the love that Christ has already secured.
He disciplines those He loves.
He calls us out of darkness because darkness is not where His children are meant to remain.
And when we stumble, our hope is not in our ability to maintain an impressive religious appearance.
Our hope is in Jesus Christ, our righteous Advocate.
So here is the question I want you to sit with.
Not for an audience.
Not for a social media reaction.
Not to impress anybody with how spiritual you sound.
Just you and God.
What is one thing in your life that Jesus has been calling you to bring into the light?
Maybe it is something you need to confess.
Maybe it is someone you need to forgive.
Maybe it is a habit you need help leaving behind.
Maybe it is the pride that has kept you from asking for prayer.
Maybe it is the exhausting performance of pretending you are spiritually healthy while your heart is starving.
Whatever it is, do not confuse hiding with healing.
And do not confuse exposure with hopelessness.
When the light of Christ reveals what is wrong, it is not because His grace has run out.
It is because His truth refuses to leave us enslaved to a lie.
You do not need to publish private details or expose someone else's sins. Even a few honest words can become an invitation for brothers and sisters in Christ to pray with you.

And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you out of shame and into a life of repentance and restoration, consider sharing it. Someone else may need to know that the grace of God is not merely a beautiful theological idea.
It changes real lives.
Please do not let this truth end with you.
Conviction calls us to turn toward Christ.
Condemnation tells us there is no hope.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
We want to keep opening the Bible, examining its original context, testing our understanding against Scripture, and pointing people back to the crucified and risen Lord.
It is not.
And not because a monthly payment can replace the wholehearted obedience, generosity, and worship that belong to a life surrendered to Jesus.
But because one meaningful way to glorify God is to use the resources He has entrusted to us to support the faithful proclamation of His Word.

If this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, strengthened your faith, encouraged you toward repentance, or reminded you of the grace of Christ, prayerfully consider helping us continue that work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not come from compulsion, but from a willing heart.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Just a sincere opportunity to take part in work you believe is honoring Christ.
These items are not the reason to give. They are simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who help sustain the ministry.
Because the Gospel itself is not merchandise.
Grace is not for sale.
Salvation cannot be bought.
And nobody should ever be made to feel that financial limitations place them farther from the love of Jesus Christ.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures for themselves.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Every sincere act of service matters, even when it comes without money or public recognition.
Because our ultimate goal is not to build a following around a personality.
It is to point people to Jesus.
The One who was rejected so that sinners could be welcomed.
The One who suffered outside the gate.
The One whose blood sanctifies His people.
The One who did not remain in the tomb.
The One who still calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness to everyone who comes to Him in faith.
Now return with me, one final time, to that wilderness camp.
The tents.
The desert.
The ordinary people.
The small shovel in someone's hand.
The simple instruction to carry waste outside the camp and cover it.
What once seemed like one of the strangest commands in Scripture now speaks with remarkable clarity.
God cared about the way His people lived because He was dwelling among them.
His holiness was not confined to a sacred building.
It shaped the entire community.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ would suffer outside the gate to sanctify a people for Himself.
The connection is not that human waste secretly represents the crucifixion.

The connection is the magnificent unfolding of Scripture's larger story: the holy God who dwelt among Israel has made a way, through Jesus Christ, for sinful human beings to be forgiven, cleansed, and brought near.
So do not leave this passage merely amused that the Bible contains instructions about human waste.
Let it remind you that God cares about the ordinary details of life.
Let it confront the places where you have separated religious appearance from genuine obedience.
Let it remind you that holiness matters.
And above all, let it lead you to Christ.
Because you cannot bury your guilt deeply enough to erase it.
You cannot perform enough religious activities to save yourself.
You cannot rewrite your past through willpower.
But you can bring your sins to Jesus in repentance and faith.
You can receive His forgiveness.
You can walk in the light.
You can begin again, not because your past was harmless, but because His grace is greater than your ability to redeem yourself.
“Jesus, make my heart holy.”
Not as a performance.
Not as a formula that earns salvation.
But as an honest cry to the Savior who makes sinners new.
And remember this when shame tries to convince you that your story is over:
The Savior who suffered outside the gate can bring home the very person who thought their shame had left them outside forever.
